displayQuote: There is no greater agony than bearing an untold story inside you

meta.title: Who really said "There is no greater agony than bearing an untold story inside you"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Widely credited to Maya Angelou, this line is actually Zora Neale Hurston’s, from her 1942 autobiography Dust Tracks on a Road.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'There is no greater agony than bearing an untold story inside you'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Maya Angelou. The line is Zora Neale Hurston’s, written in her 1942 memoir Dust Tracks on a Road — and slightly reworded over the years.

answer.label: Not Maya Angelou — actually Zora Neale Hurston
answer.authorDates: 1891–1960 · writer, anthropologist and folklorist of the Harlem Renaissance
answer.sourceLine: The line comes from Hurston’s 1942 autobiography Dust Tracks on a Road, where she wrote “There is no agony like bearing an untold story inside you.” It is pervasively — but wrongly — credited to Maya Angelou’s I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings (1969), usually in the slightly reworded “no greater agony than” form.

source.heading: Where the line really comes from

docMeta.dd: “There is no agony like bearing an untold story inside you”

source.excerpt: … the force from somewhere in Space which commands you to write in the first place, gives you no choice. You take up the pen when you are told, and write what is commanded. There is no agony like bearing an untold story inside you. You have all heard of the Spartan youth with the fox under his cloak.
trail: Quote Investigator locates the sentence in Hurston’s Dust Tracks on a Road (1942) and finds citations correctly crediting Hurston as early as 1997.
WIST Quotations records the exact line under Hurston, Dust Tracks on a Road (1942), and flags that it is “sometimes misattributed to Maya Angelou.”
The reworded version circulates under Angelou on Goodreads with tens of thousands of likes, tagged to I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings — where the sentence does not appear.
source.cutTag: ↑ the viral “greater agony than” wording reworks Hurston’s original “agony like”
source.excerptNote: The sentence sits inside a meditation on the compulsion to write. Note the original reads “no agony like” — the widely shared Angelou version smooths it to “no greater agony than.”

source.rightsNote: Hurston’s Dust Tracks on a Road (1942) remains under U.S. copyright, so the sentence is not public domain. Quote it with attribution to Zora Neale Hurston, not Maya Angelou.

author.name: Zora Neale Hurston
author.heading: About Zora Neale Hurston
author.bio: Zora Neale Hurston was a central figure of the Harlem Renaissance and a pioneering Black anthropologist and folklorist. Best known for the novel Their Eyes Were Watching God (1937), she published her autobiography Dust Tracks on a Road in 1942. She died in relative obscurity in 1960; her reputation was later revived largely through the advocacy of Alice Walker in the 1970s.

copyAttribution: There is no agony like bearing an untold story inside you. —Zora Neale Hurston, Dust Tracks on a Road (1942). Frequently misattributed to Maya Angelou.

misattribution.heading: The misattribution
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most durable author mix-ups online: two Black women autobiographers, both writing about the pain of the unspoken, separated by a generation.

items.why: It is routinely tagged to Angelou’s I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings (1969) — e.g. on Goodreads and BrainyQuote — but the sentence predates that memoir by 27 years and appears in Hurston, not Angelou. QuotePark notes the same: ‘actually from Zora Neale Hurston.’

misattribution.truthLine: The words are Zora Neale Hurston’s, from Dust Tracks on a Road (1942): “There is no agony like bearing an untold story inside you.”

context.heading: Why the mix-up stuck
lead: The confusion is almost poetic. Both Hurston and Angelou wrote landmark autobiographies about finding a voice under the weight of silence, so a line about the agony of an untold story feels equally at home with either name attached.

Angelou’s far greater late-century fame acted as an attribution magnet: as the sentence spread on quote sites and social media, it drifted toward the better-known author and picked up a smoother wording along the way.
detailsBody: Hurston’s original construction is “no agony like.” The version that went viral under Angelou’s name is “no greater agony than” — a common signature of a quote that has been passed hand to hand and quietly polished rather than copied from the page.
